mcqs.question: Why does 0/1 knapsack need a 2D state (item, capacity) instead of the 1D shape used by House Robber?
options: Because knapsack always has more items than a typical House Robber input
Because knapsack requires sorting the items first
Because the answer for a given capacity depends on which items remain available, and capacity alone doesn't determine that
Because a 1D array cannot represent weights larger than a certain size
mcqs.explanation: One index (capacity) can't distinguish 'best value reachable with these specific items available' from a different item set that reaches the same capacity — the answer genuinely depends on two independent facts, so both must be part of the state.

mcqs.question: In the space-optimized 1D version of 0/1 knapsack, why does iterating capacity forward (low to high) cause an item to be reused?
options: Forward iteration is always slower, which is the only downside
It causes an off-by-one in the capacity bounds, not a reuse bug

By the time a larger capacity is computed, a smaller capacity's cell may already reflect this same item having been taken in this same pass, since the 1D array no longer separates 'before' from 'after' this item
Forward iteration only affects unbounded knapsack, not 0/1
mcqs.explanation: The 1D array collapses two logical rows into one, so forward iteration risks reading a cell already updated by the current item in this same pass — silently allowing that item to contribute twice. Iterating backward guarantees every read cell still holds the previous row's value.

mcqs.question: What single change converts the 1D 0/1 knapsack solution into the 1D unbounded knapsack solution?
options: Sorting items by weight before the main loop
Adding a second dimension to track how many copies of each item were used
Replacing max() with sum() in the recurrence
Reversing the capacity loop's direction from backward to forward, so a reachable cell can reflect the current item already being reused
mcqs.explanation: Flipping capacity iteration from backward to forward lets a cell's own update from earlier in the same pass be read again, which is exactly the reuse unbounded knapsack allows. No extra dimension, sort, or operator change is needed — it really is that one-line difference.

mcqs.question: How does subset-sum relate to 0/1 knapsack?
options: It's an entirely unrelated problem that happens to also use a 2D table
It's 0/1 knapsack with values dropped — the table becomes a boolean 'is this sum reachable' using the same take-or-skip recurrence over weights
It's 0/1 knapsack solved with a greedy algorithm instead of DP
It's the unbounded knapsack variant applied to a single target capacity
mcqs.explanation: Subset-sum only cares about reachability, not value, so the value axis collapses into a boolean per (item, sum) cell, but the take-or-skip recurrence over the weight/target axis is identical to ordinary 0/1 knapsack's.
